title: Kernel contracts and coordinator notes
content:
Context / motivation:
We keep iterating on heterogeneous kernel execution (TensorRT, Triton-hosted models, and our in-house custom ops). Past experiments focused on perf but not on the runtime-level interface stability required for safe live kernel swaps. This doc collects notes on a minimal kernel contract, coordinator behavior for routing/fallbacks, and KV-cache consistency checks we should run before/after kernel transitions.

High-level goals:
- Define a small, testable contract shape that any kernel adapter must implement.
- Make coordinator decisions deterministic and auditable (why we chose a kernel, why we swapped).
- Ensure KV cache remains coherent across kernel switches (no silent quality regressions).
- Provide observability hooks and perf regression thresholds to auto-fallback.

Problems we've seen in experiments (root causes and examples):
- Silent numeric drift: INT8/Tensorrt kernels with asymmetric quantization cause tiny differences in logits that break rerankers (observed +0.6% avg-churn on top-10 in a rerank workload).
- KV layout mismatch: custom-kernel used a different packed kv layout; on swap we saw 1.2x memory spike and OOMs during long-context evals.
- Warmup latency cliff: Triton-backed model takes ~1.1s to JIT/compile on first request; coordinator routed too many traffic into it and violated p99 SLO.
- Eviction mismatch: some kernels expect the runtime to evict per-layer caches independently; others require contiguous buffer ownership. Swapping without migration caused stale pointers.

Proposed minimal kernel capability descriptor (returned at registration / handshake) — contract fields (textual):
- kernel_id: stable string identifier
- supported_precisions: comma list (fp32, fp16, int8-wq, int8-aq)
- max_sequence: integer
- supports_streaming: true|false
- kv_serialization_checksum: hex string (schema versioned)
- kv_layout_hint: string ("per_layer_packed"|"interleaved_dense"|"sharded_by_head")
- state_migration_endpoint: text name for optional migration RPC (if present, coordinator will call before swap)
- warmup_penalty_ms: estimated cold-warm additional latency per call
- per_token_peak_gpu_mb: number (for admission control)
- observable_metrics: list of metric keys (e.g., kernel_decode_tokens, kernel_faults)

Why these fields:
- checksum and layout_hint let the coordinator decide whether a blind swap is safe or migration is required.
- warmup_penalty_ms is conservative but prevents SLO violations when switching to cold kernels.
- observable_metrics allow built-in alerting/auto-fallback rules to be generic across adapters.

Coordinator swap protocol (sequence):
1) LOADINTENT: coordinator announces intent to route N requests to kernel K and asks for current kv_serialization_checksum.
2) VALIDATE: compare checksums and kv_layout_hint. If exact match -> blind-swap allowed.
3) MIGRATE: if checksums differ but state_migration_endpoint present -> call migration RPC to translate/pack KV cache (async, with progress).
4) WARMUP: trigger warmup runner with small synthetic requests (bounded by warmup_penalty_ms budget).
5) CUTOVER: atomically switch routing table entry to new kernel, tag trace/span with swap_id and reason.
6) MONITOR: for 60s post-cutover evaluate p50/p90/p99 and application-level quality signals (perplexity, top-k stability).
7) ROLLBACK: if any threshold exceeded, rollback to previous kernel and mark new kernel as degraded for cooldown window.

Performance thresholds / heuristics (initial values to tune):
- Acceptable perf regression: p99 latency increase <= 15% and throughput drop <= 10% over baseline for 60s window.
- Quality guard: application-level drift (task-specific metric) <= 0.5% relative. E.g., rerank top-1 churn <= 1%.
- Memory guard: peak GPU memory <= reserved_capacity * 1.05.
- Faults guard: kernel_faults > 0 -> immediate rollback.

KV cache safety modes (operator-level):
- STRICT: only allow swap if checksum exact match. Use for high-sensitivity workloads (LLMs that condition long contexts).
- MIGRATE: allow swap if migration endpoint exists; migration performed live with backpressure.
- BEST_EFFORT: allow blind swap and reconstruct KV on-demand from input prompts (acceptable for stateless or short-context workloads).

Observed bench numbers (sanity-check experiments, microbench harness v0.9):
- Setup: Mistral-like 7B decoder, sequence=2048, batch=1 streaming decode. Baselines on A100-40GB.
- Triton fp16 (server): p50=2.8ms/token, p99=6.4ms/token, warmup=1100ms cold compile.
- TensorRT fp16 optimized: p50=2.1ms/token, p99=4.2ms/token, warmup=40ms (kernel graph warmup).
- TensorRT int8 (wq): p50=1.5ms/token, p99=3.8ms/token, observed top-10 rerank-churn +0.9% (numeric drift).
- Custom-kernel (layer-fused, batching-friendly): p50=1.9ms, p99=5.0ms, but per_token_peak_gpu_mb +12% vs Triton.
- Blind-swap between TRT-int8 -> Triton-fp16 during long-context stream caused a transient 0.3% token duplication in tests (edge-case bug from kv indexing).

Tradeoffs summary (short):
- Perf-first kernels (TRT-int8) give best latency/throughput but increase numeric drift risk and require strict evaluation per workload.
- Triton-hosted FP16 has best compatibility and easier rollback but higher latency and compiler cold-start cost.
- Custom kernels let us control memory layout and KV packing but increase maintenance and fragmentation risk (divergent contracts).

Testing harness recommendations:
- Add a "swap smoke" suite running on CI that performs kernel swap during long streaming decode (sequence=2048, 5 swaps across 10s) and validates token-level checksum and rerank consistency.
- Add quantized golden sets: small prompt sets where we measure top-k stability, perplexity, and token drift across precisions.
- Simulate partial migration failures (cut network mid-migration) to validate rollback logic and garbage-collection of partial migrated state.

Observability hooks we need in runtime/console:
- swap_events stream (swap_id, from_kernel, to_kernel, reason, outcome).
- kernel_capabilities registry view (live capabilities, last_seen, degraded_flag).
- kv_layout_mismatch rate and migration duration histogram.
- quality_signal metrics mapping per-route (confluence page will define metric names).

Open questions / decision points:
- Do we require all adapters to implement migration endpoint, or make it optional? (I lean optional but strongly encouraged; put migration interface in SDK).
- How much warmup budget should the coordinator keep per route? static budget vs adaptive (learned) budget?
- Should we support online kv-format translation as a fallback in Best_Effort mode (reconstructing only missing keys) vs full migration?
- Where to surface kernel capability differences in the Console UX to help SREs decide rollouts?

Action items / next experiments:
- [ ] Implement capability descriptor v1 in kernel-adapter SDK (owner: Miguel) — include checksum util and layout_hint enum.
- [ ] Add a CI swap-smoke case and run across the 3 adapters (owner: Samantha) — record regression rates.
- [ ] Build a small migration prototype for the per_layer_packed -> interleaved_dense case and measure migration time for seq=4096 contexts (owner: Owen).
- [ ] Add swap_events telemetry + console table prototype (owner: Asha).

Notes to self: keep this doc lightweight and iterate. The goal is a pragmatic contract that prevents the worst failure modes (OOMs, silent quality regression, warmup SLO bursts) while not blocking every potentially useful kernel.

References & links:
- experiment traces: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/ci/swap-smoke/logs/2025-11-12
- prototype migration PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/842
- related spec: confluence.redwood.com/display/RT/kv-cache-shapes (draft)

If we agree on the capability descriptor shape I can sketch the JSON schema and the adapter SDK stub tomorrow.
